Assume <MATH_0001> is dominant.
Say <MATH_0002> is the decomposition
of <MATH_0003> into irreducible components. Let <MATH_0004> be
its generic point, so <MATH_0005>.
Note that <MATH_0006> is an irreducible subset of <MATH_0007>.
Hence
<MATH_0008>
is a finite union of irreducible subsets whose generic
points are in the image of <MATH_0009>. The lemma follows.

Let <MATH_0001> be a morphism of integral schemes. The following
are equivalent
<STRUCT_0001>
<STRUCT_0002> <MATH_0002> is dominant,
<STRUCT_0003> <MATH_0003> maps the generic point of <MATH_0004> to the generic point of <MATH_0005>,
<STRUCT_0004> for some nonempty affine opens <MATH_0006> and <MATH_0007>
with <MATH_0008> the ring map <MATH_0009>
is injective,
<STRUCT_0005> for all nonempty affine opens <MATH_0010> and <MATH_0011>
with <MATH_0012> the ring map <MATH_0013>
is injective,
<STRUCT_0006> for some <MATH_0014> with image <MATH_0015> the local ring
map <MATH_0016> is injective, and
<STRUCT_0007> for all <MATH_0017> with image <MATH_0018> the local ring
map <MATH_0019> is injective.
<STRUCT_0008>

The equivalence of (1) and (2) follows from
Lemma <REF_0001>.
Let <MATH_0001> and <MATH_0002> be nonempty affine opens with
<MATH_0003>. Recall that the rings <MATH_0004>
and <MATH_0005> are integral domains.
The morphism <MATH_0006> corresponds to a ring map
<MATH_0007>. The generic points of <MATH_0008> and <MATH_0009> correspond
to the prime ideals <MATH_0010> and <MATH_0011>. Thus
(2) is equivalent to the condition <MATH_0012>,
i.e., to the condition that <MATH_0013> is injective.
In this way we see that (2), (3), and (4) are equivalent.
Similarly, given <MATH_0014> and <MATH_0015> as in (5) the local rings
<MATH_0016> and <MATH_0017> are domains
and the prime ideals <MATH_0018>
and <MATH_0019> correspond to the
generic points of <MATH_0020> and <MATH_0021> (via the identification of
the spectrum of the local ring at <MATH_0022>
with the set of points specializing to <MATH_0023>, see
Schemes, Lemma <REF_0002>).
Thus we can argue in the exact same manner as above
to see that (2), (5), and (6) are equivalent.
